Bate's assured leadership of the ENO Orchestra on top form playing Gluck's rhythmic Bach-meets-Mozart music, which made the transition between baroque and classical opera in the second half of the 18th century, transports us to another realm.
Turner’s production is understated and ideal.
They give Iphigénie en Tauride the best possible chance, but the result is still something of a disappointment.
The result isn't flawless, but it's an absorbing and frequently thrilling evening, distinguished by exceptional conducting, superb orchestral playing and some outstanding singing.
In its best moments, this production is blissful.
Lyndsey Turner's unpretentious production of Iphigénie en Tauride succeeds on most levels and engages the heart in ways no amount of reimagined faffing could hope to do.
Its uncertain opening and confusing visual choices are frustrating, but the later acts bring the acting, lighting, ensemble and music together with spectacular effect.
The artists' well-deserved praise cannot be separated from Gluck's adaptation and Guillard's libretto, with its greater emphasis on subtle emotional suffering.

cn.t: ENO's rare staging of Gluck's masterpiece wins praise for Christine Rice's lyrical performance and David Bates' exceptional conducting, though critics split on Lyndsey Turner's minimalist production—some find it elegantly spare, others disappointingly austere.
